teaser.text: Interactive Brokers Group (IBKR) is an electronic brokerage: it gives investors and financial firms a way to trade investments around the world and keep them in one account. Its business becomes clear when you follow a dollar through that account—first as a customer’s money, then as a fee, interest payment or financing balance, and finally as revenue left after costs.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for Interactive Brokers Group?

paragraphs.text: The base case assumes steady growth, moderate dilution, gradual dividend increases and some valuation compression.

Bear revenue is $7,600 million in the first year and $7,900 million in the second. Margin falls from 17.0% to 16.5%, so earnings reach $1,304 million before settling at $1,312 million on final revenue of $8,200 million and a 16.0% margin. The bull case begins with $8,200 million of revenue and reaches $9,840 million in the second year. Final revenue is $11,800 million, with margin rising from 19.0% to 20.0%; earnings reach $1,919 million and then $2,360 million. The spread reflects rate exposure: a 25-basis-point move changes annual NII by $83 million. Softer activity also matters, as annualized cleared DARTs per account fell from 213 to 203.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Interactive Brokers Group really make?

paragraphs.text: Operating cash flow reached $15,811 million in 2025, including a $38,993 million increase in amounts payable to customers. After $67 million of capital spending, reported free cash flow was $15,744 million. Its 253.7% margin is therefore an accounting signal to investigate, not money that can simply be paid out.

IBKR’s “real free cash flow” subtracts $118 million of stock compensation and comes to $15,626 million. That subtraction recognizes dilution’s economic cost, but it does not remove customer obligations, restricted cash, regulatory capital needs or earnings belonging to other owners.

blocks.heading: What has Interactive Brokers Group guided for rates?

paragraphs.text: Using balances at September 30, 2026, management estimated that a 25-basis-point move in the US Federal Reserve’s benchmark rate would change annual NII by $83 million. A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, so 25 basis points equals 0.25%. This is an annual sensitivity, not a forecast of the next quarter’s profit.

The international effect matters too. Management estimated a separate $35 million annual NII effect from an equivalent move in relevant non-US rates. As customers, balances and currencies change, the old sensitivity becomes less reliable. That makes the rate guide useful, but only as a starting point for the earnings outlook.

blocks.heading: Did Interactive Brokers Group keep its growth promise?

paragraphs.text: Management reported more than one million new accounts during 2025 and a record annual pretax margin of 77%. Those results support its broad promise to pursue growth while controlling technology costs, but they do not show that executives met undisclosed bonus thresholds.

blocks.heading: What do Interactive Brokers Group’s last eight quarters show?

paragraphs.text: Revenue reached $1,914 million, up 15.6% from a year earlier. Pretax income rose to $1,496 million, an increase of 14.0%. Common-shareholder income rose from $263 million to $314 million, while diluted earnings per share rose from $0.59 to $0.69.

blocks.heading: What should Interactive Brokers Group watchers look for next?

paragraphs.text: A further product milestone came on the October 15 call. CEO Milan Galik said IBKR aimed to offer Cboe’s single-stock event contracts, with a possible exchange launch near the end of October but unsettled timing. The important evidence will be actual IBKR availability and repeated customer trading.
